theory.intro: The **population** is every individual or item being investigated. A **census** collects data from the whole population; a **sample** collects data from part of it. Name the population first — the same data can be a census of one and a sample of another.
facts: The **population** is every individual or item being investigated — not just the ones who ended up being surveyed.
A census can cover millions of people — a large population does **not** make a study a sample.
What matters is whether **everyone** in the population was included, not how many people there are.
A sample is used when the population is too large, or when a census would cost too much or take too long.
When testing uses up an item or leaves it unfit for sale, testing a sample keeps the rest available to sell.
A census covers the whole population. Data still need to be measured and recorded correctly; including everyone does not guarantee an error-free result.

workedExamples.question_text:
A museum wants to know what its Saturday visitors think of a new display.
(a) It asks every visitor who attends on Saturday.
(b) It asks only every fourth visitor who attends on Saturday.
State the population and classify each collection as a census or a sample.
workedExamples.solution_text:
In both cases, the population is **all visitors who attend the museum on Saturday**.
(a) Every member of that population is asked, so this is a **census**.
(b) Only part of that population is asked, so this is a **sample**.
The classification depends on whether the whole defined group is included.

workedExamples.question_text:
All $26$ members of a school gardening club give their opinions about a new canteen menu. The school has $684$ students.
(a) A report describes what the gardening club members think.
(b) Another report uses the same answers to describe what all students at the school think.
State the population and classify the collection for each report.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The population is **all $26$ gardening club members**. Every one gives an answer, so the collection is a **census** of the club.
(b) The population is **all $684$ students at the school**. Only the $26$ club members give answers, so the collection is a **sample** of the school.
The answers are the same, but the population being investigated is different.

workedExamples.question_text:
Choose a census or a sample in each situation and explain why.
(a) A teacher needs the height of each of the $23$ students in a class to order costumes.
(b) A biscuit factory checks strength by crushing biscuits. Biscuits must remain whole to be sold.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Use a **census** of the class. Measure all $23$ students because each costume needs its own measurement. An estimate from only a few students would not give the needed height for every student.
(b) Test a **sample** from the biscuits produced. Crushing every biscuit would leave none whole for sale. Testing only part of the population leaves the other biscuits available to sell.

workedExamples.question_text:
A council wants residents' views on a new park. It interviews $180$ of the town's $22700$ residents because interviewing everyone would cost too much and take too long.
Leah calls this a census because the report is about the whole town.
State the population, explain Leah's mistake and explain why a sample was chosen.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The population is **all $22700$ residents of the town**.
Only $180$ residents are interviewed, so this is a **sample**.
Leah has confused the group the report is about with the group actually asked. A census would need data from every resident. The size of the population alone does not decide the classification.
A sample was chosen because asking only part of the population takes less time and costs less than asking everyone.

foundation.question_text:
Data is collected from **every** member of the population.
What name is given to this type of data collection?
foundation.solution_text:
Data comes from the whole population.
**A census.**

foundation.question_text:
Data is collected from only **part** of the population.
What name is given to this type of data collection?
foundation.solution_text:
Data comes from part of the population.
**A sample.**

foundation.question_text:
A school with $940$ students gives its lunch-quality survey to every student in the school, to find out what the school's students think.
Is this a census or a sample?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all $940$ students at the school.
Every one of them was surveyed.
**Census.**

foundation.question_text:
One Year $8$ class of $28$ students is surveyed to find out what all $940$ students at the school think of the lunches.
Is this a census or a sample?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all $940$ students at the school.
Only $28$ of them were surveyed.
**Sample.**

foundation.question_text:
Scientists tag and track $200$ of the $3500$ humpback whales in Australian waters to study their migration.
Is this a census or a sample?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all $3500$ whales.
Only $200$ of them were tracked.
**Sample.**

foundation.question_text:
Every five years the Australian Government collects information from every resident of Australia.
Is this a census or a sample?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is every resident of Australia.
Information is collected from all of them.
**Census.**

foundation.question_text:
An automatic scale on a factory line weighs every jar of sauce produced during a shift.
Is this a census or a sample of that shift's jars?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is every jar produced during the shift.
All of them are weighed.
**Census.**

foundation.question_text:
A phone factory takes every tenth screen off the line and tests it for scratches.
Is this a census or a sample?
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all the screens produced.
Only every tenth screen is tested.
**Sample.**

development.question_text:
A ranger examines $60$ of the little penguins in a colony to check the health of the colony. These are some, but not all, of the colony's little penguins.
State the population, and whether this is a census or a sample.
development.solution_text:
Population: **all the little penguins in the colony**.
Only $60$ of them were examined.
**Sample.**

development.question_text:
A helmet factory crash-tests $20$ helmets taken from a batch of $5000$ before the batch is sold.
State the population, and whether this is a census or a sample.
development.solution_text:
Population: **all $5000$ helmets in the batch**.
Only $20$ of them were tested.
**Sample.**

development.question_text:
A carnival organiser wants to know which sports **Year $7$ students** want at the carnival, and asks all $120$ Year $7$ students at the school.
State the population, and whether this is a census or a sample.
development.solution_text:
Population: **all $120$ Year $7$ students**.
Every one of them was asked.
**Census.**

development.question_text:
In a school of $800$ students, the SRC asks all $150$ Year $9$ students about canteen prices and reports what **the whole school** thinks.
State the population, and whether this is a census or a sample.
development.solution_text:
Population: **all $800$ students at the school**.
Only the $150$ Year $9$ students were asked.
**Sample.**

development.question_text:
A sauce factory checks that jars are sealed correctly by opening a jar and testing its seal. The remaining jars must stay sealed for sale.
Explain why the factory should use a sample rather than a census.
development.solution_text:
Opening a jar breaks its seal, so that jar cannot be sold as sealed.
A census would mean opening every jar, leaving no sealed jars to sell.
**A sample should be used.**

development.question_text:
A teacher wants the average time her class of $25$ students spent on homework last night.
Should she use a census or a sample?
Justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
The population is only the $25$ students in the class.
Asking all $25$ is quick and uses the whole class to calculate the average instead of estimating it from only part of the class.
**A census.**

development.question_text:
The national census is run only once every five years rather than every year.
Give one reason why a government would not collect data from every resident more often.
development.solution_text:
Collecting and processing an answer from every single resident costs an enormous amount of money and takes a long time.
**Cost and time are why a census of a whole country is run only rarely.**

mastery.question_text:
Marcus says the Australian Census cannot really be a census, because $26$ million people is far too many for anyone to collect data from everyone.
Explain why Marcus is incorrect, and describe what would make the collection a sample instead.
mastery.solution_text:
Whether a collection is a census depends on **who is included**, not on how large the population is.
The Census collects data from every resident of Australia, so it covers the whole population.
It would only be a sample if data were collected from part of the population — for example, from $10\,000$ selected households.
**A large population does not turn a census into a sample.**

mastery.question_text:
A match factory tests match quality by striking matches to see whether they light. Untested matches are needed for sale.
Explain why a census would be unsuitable here, and describe a sample the quality team could take instead.
mastery.solution_text:
Striking a match uses it up, so the tested match cannot be sold.
A census would mean striking every match the factory makes, leaving none to sell.
Instead the team could strike a few matches from selected boxes, such as $5$ matches from every hundredth box.
**Testing a sample leaves the other matches available to sell.**

mastery.question_text:
A ranger counts every one of the $74$ koalas living inside a fenced sanctuary.
The sanctuary manager wants to know how many koalas live in the sanctuary, while a state scientist wants to know how many koalas live in the whole state.
Explain why the same count is a census for one of them and a sample for the other.
mastery.solution_text:
For the manager the population is the $74$ koalas in the sanctuary, and all $74$ of them were counted, so the count is a **census**.
For the scientist the population is every koala in the state, and the sanctuary koalas are only a small part of it, so the same count is a **sample**.
The label depends on the population being investigated, not on how the data was gathered.
